analysis.one_liner: Funds free lawyers for low-income tenants facing eviction.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Financial Services Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a competitive grant program at the Department of Housing and Urban Development to pay nonprofits and government agencies to give free legal help to low-income tenants facing eviction [S2] [S3]. Tenants earning under roughly 135% of the federal poverty line would qualify [S3]. Grants would be steered toward high-eviction neighborhoods, areas with strong tenant-protection laws, and rural communities [S3]. The bill was introduced in February 2020, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never taken up [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income tenants at risk of eviction would get a lawyer at no cost to represent them in court, negotiate settlements, and contest evictions; studies of right-to-counsel programs show representation sharply reduces the odds an unrepresented tenant loses their home by default. Nonprofit legal aid organizations would gain federal funding to expand their staff.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a HUD grant program so eligible tenants get legal assistance at no cost, covering pretrial, trial, post-trial, and mediation work [S3].
Eligibility is targeted to low-income tenants — households at or below 135% of the federal poverty guidelines or below a rent-based income test tied to local fair market rent [S3].
A preference system directs grants to census tracts with high eviction rates and to jurisdictions whose laws protect tenants (right to counsel, habitability, security-deposit limits) [S3].
A rural-equity provision requires that rural tenants receive legal aid at least in proportion to their share of eligible tenants [S3].
Grantees must report how many evictions were avoided or resolved on better terms, and provide demographic data, creating public accountability for the spending [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the grants; the bill sets no dollar amount and includes no appropriation authorization, leaving the size of the program to future spending bills. Landlords would face tenants who, for the first time in many eviction courts, have legal representation — making quick default judgments and rubber-stamp evictions harder.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and landlords in eviction disputes

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes no specific funding level, so as written it mandates a program without committing dollars to it [S3].

A good-faith objection: taxpayer-funded lawyers on one side of eviction cases raises costs and slows court proceedings for landlords, including small property owners, and some argue mediation or rental assistance could prevent evictions at lower cost than full legal representation [S3].

The competitive point system — favoring high-eviction tracts and jurisdictions with certain tenant laws — could leave equally needy tenants in low-eviction or weak-tenant-protection areas with less access to help [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tenants it covers, the benefit is concrete and well documented: an unrepresented tenant in eviction court usually loses, often by default, and counsel changes that. The main costs are the federal dollars (unquantified in the bill) and slower, more contested eviction proceedings for landlords. The eligibility line and preference formulas are reasonable but arbitrary at the edges. On balance, this is a narrowly targeted, low-risk program whose costs are modest relative to the stakes for the families it reaches.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never considered it, so it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Representative James Clyburn introduced the Legal Assistance to Prevent Evictions Act on February 13, 2020, joined by four original cosponsors [S1] [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day [S5].
No further action was recorded — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords, who continue to face mostly unrepresented tenants in eviction court, and the federal treasury, which never funded the program. Low-income tenants at risk of eviction are no better off than before.

for.name: Rep. James Clyburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited four original cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. David Price, Yvette Clarke, Ro Khanna, and Jahana Hayes
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Rep. Maxine Waters, D-CA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving the bill without any committee action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: No House Republican cosponsored the bill and it received no floor consideration in the GOP-held Senate or from House leadership.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the House never went on record; support was entirely Democratic — all 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats — and no Republican signed on [S4].

industries.industry: Civil legal aid and legal services nonprofits
industries.note: The bill would make experienced nonprofit legal aid organizations the permanent channel for federal eviction-defense funding, with a preference for providers who already do this work. Their mission — keeping low-income tenants housed — runs alongside tenants' interests.

Tenants with lawyers are far more likely to contest evictions, negotiate settlements, or win on habitability defenses, ending the routine of default judgments against unrepresented tenants. Small landlords bear the same added cost as large ones.
